title: FAI investigates alleged racist abuse of Idah
description: The FAI is amassing high-quality footage of the alleged incident with the aim of presenting evidence to Uefa.
fullText:
The Football Association of Ireland is investigating whether forward Adam Idah was racially abused by Israel supporters during Sunday's 3-0 Uefa Nations League victory for the Republic of Ireland.

BBC Sport understands that midfielder Jayson Molumby spoke to the match officials during play, asking them to listen out for what he believed to be abusive chanting coming from some of the small number of Israel fans present at the match.

After full-time the officials informed FAI staff members that they did not subsequently hear any racist chanting.

When the FAI spoke to the Uefa match delegate about the alleged incident, they were informed that because no clear allegation of racism was reported during the game, the normal protocols had not been followed and a Uefa investigation could not take place.

The FAI is now conducting its own investigation by amassing high-quality footage of the match, including audio from pitchside microphones, in order to establish whether or not abuse was directed at Idah.

A panel is being set up by the FAI to analyse the footage and audio recordings. If the panel believes there is evidence to suggest Idah was abused, it will make a complaint to Uefa and request a further investigation by European football's governing body.

Idah was unaware of any possible abuse during the match and is now being supported by team-mates and staff members before the Republic of Ireland's remaining three fixtures in the current international break.

It is unclear whether the FAI would present its case to Uefa before or after Sunday's behind-closed-doors game against Israel in Backa Topola, Serbia.

BBC Sport has contacted Uefa for comment.

Republic of Ireland 'raised awareness worldwide' in Israel game

FAI unclear over possible sanctions if game not played

Republic of Ireland defeat Israel in Debrecen

Swansea City player Idah scored the second goal in a match which had been in doubt in the run-up to kick off, amid widespread protests against facing Israel from Irish fans and politicians, and late discussions among the playing squad about whether or not to fulfil the fixture.

The game was held in the city of Debrecen, Hungary, with about 300 Israel supporters present and no tickets sold to Irish fans, though a handful did manage to enter the stadium

The second fixture in Serbia this Sunday is a 'home' match for the Republic of Ireland but has been moved to a remote corner of Europe amid ongoing protests from fans over the FAI's decision to fulfil the fixtures.

The FAI voted earlier this year to play the matches, having been concerned about potential sanctions, including fines and expulsions from competitions, if it had opted to boycott.

Ireland has been among the European countries to most keenly show support for Palestinians since the start of Israel's military offensive in Gaza in October 2023.

More than 73,000 people have been killed in Israeli attacks, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.

The FAI has asked Uefa to keep the Republic of Ireland and Israel apart in future draws.

The two teams did not shake hands or exchange pennants before the match kicked off, and the Irish team bowed their heads during the Israeli national anthem.

After scoring the third goal, winger Jack Moylan held up and kissed a black armband the Republic of Ireland players were wearing "in recognition of all lives lost in the conflict".

Goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu withdrew from the squad following a long meeting held in the hotel, when the match appeared to be in jeopardy as training and the pre-match news conference were repeatedly delayed.

Bazunu said in a statement on social media: "I am a man of strong faith, and try my best to be a person of character and principle. Therefore I feel it would be wrong to participate in the upcoming fixtures against Israel."

Bazunu has returned to the squad for Thursday's match against Austria in Dublin, but will be absent again for the second game against Israel.

Israel captain Manor Solomon said: "I'm waiting for the next game against them - it will be a completely different game entirely.

"They don't interest me. We have a country 10 times better than theirs - stronger, an amazing country with amazing people.

"We are proud to wear the team shirt and to be Israelis. We are proud of our state and of our soldiers.

"They can play all their tricks. We are Israelis and love the country. And that will always be the case.

"If I say what I think of them, I would likely be suspended for a few matches. Obviously they hate us. We don't like them."

title: Could Potter be England's next breakthrough star?
description: With Sarina Wiegman set to name her latest England squad on Tuesday, there is one name everyone is talking about - Lexi Potter. Here is why.
fullText:
With Sarina Wiegman set to name her latest England squad on Tuesday, there is one name everyone is talking about.

The 20-year-old Chelsea midfielder has been a standout performer in the Women's Super League this season and has staked a claim to earn her first senior call-up.

After steady performances against Manchester United and Birmingham City, she caught everyone's attention with an impressive display against rivals Arsenal.

Potter helped Chelsea to a 1-0 victory and a third successive league clean sheet as she looked right at home among England's elite.

Former Lionesses striker Ellen White said Potter was "a special player", while Chelsea team-mate Lucy Bronze believed she could be the next Keira Walsh.

So why is everyone so excited about Potter and is she ready to join the England squad for the first time this week?

Chelsea restore resilience - are they title contenders again?

Potter's performance against Arsenal was the latest in a string of displays that have pleased manager Sonia Bompastor.

The Chelsea academy graduate broke through last season, scoring the winner on her first WSL start against Brighton in March.

It came after a two-year spell on loan at Crystal Palace where she gained regular first-team football and has already notched up 20 appearances.

This season Potter has stepped up, starting alongside England midfielder Walsh in three of Chelsea's four WSL matches.

Their partnership is flourishing and it has allowed Walsh to push further up the pitch and provide a goalscoring threat for the Blues.

Their winner against Arsenal came as a result of Walsh's saved shot falling to the feet of Alyssa Thompson, while Potter herself scored in the 2-0 victory over Birmingham.

When asked about Potter's impact, Bompastor said: "I was really happy with Lexi last season, though she probably didn't get as many opportunities as this season.

"For her age, being able to be consistent and in the way that she has been performing, I think it's great.

"People were probably looking at [the Arsenal game] to see her in a big occasion and whether she was able to repeat and sustain the performance.

"I think she proved that she can. Keira [Walsh] is playing at that level because she has more freedom to go forward by having Lexi next to her."

Potter has shown immense composure on the ball and maintained a 93% passing accuracy in the WSL so far this season.

She ranks fourth among her team-mates in tackles and interceptions and has the third-best passing success rate at Chelsea.

The midfielder has already played 207 minutes, made 21 recoveries in the WSL and is yet to be on the pitch while her side have conceded a goal this term.

It's clear she is making an impact.

"Chelsea have spent a lot of money on players in that team but she has grabbed the opportunity," ex-England striker White told the Women's Football Weekly podcast.

"It seems like she is really learning from Keira Walsh and players around her in the environment. She is growing game by game and has great physicality.

"There was one point in the Arsenal game where she had three players around her and she just flicked it around the corner to Ellie Carpenter.

"That's special to do when you're that age."

Potter has slotted into the number six position at Chelsea, provided defensive cover for Walsh and shown she can play her way out under pressure.

She has similar traits to Walsh, who has been a significant figure for England since her debut in 2017 and has over 100 caps for Wiegman's side.

One of the biggest questions surrounding Walsh has been whether anyone was capable of filling in her shoes when the 29-year-old eventually moves on.

Potter's emergence suggests she is next in line - but in the meantime, could she develop a successful partnership with Walsh in England's midfield?

"We have been crying out for someone who maybe is the next Keira Walsh. The number six position is a really difficult one to play in," added White.

"Keira has been doing it so well for so many years and is now getting better this season. She has stepped up and maybe Lexi is pushing her.

"To have Lexi in the England fold, gaining experience in the senior squad would be brilliant to see. She looks really special."

The Lionesses are hoping to secure qualification for next year's Women's World Cup in Brazil with a double-header against Greece in October.

After beating Arsenal, Chelsea boss Bompastor joked that she wished Potter could be French and believed she was ready for the international stage.

England defender Bronze, 34, added on BBC Radio 5 Live: "I'm not the manager and Sarina [Wiegman] will make her choices but Lexi has been absolutely fantastic.

"She was last year too. I remember my first season at Chelsea and seeing her train at the level she was...

"Having a player like Keira to look up to, and base her style off and learn from, you can see in every game they are developing into the same player.

"If England have another Keira Walsh, it puts us in a very good position!"

title: Republicans join Democrats in questioning Trump's taxpayer-funded TV ads
description: A screenshot of President Donald Trump's 2023 ad for the 2024 presidential elections. —Screenshot from Donald Trump's Truth Social account...
fullText:
President Donald Trump declares that “this is the final battle” in one of several taxpayer-funded television ads airing ahead of November’s midterm elections, prompting bipartisan scrutiny over whether the spots violate federal law.

The 30-second ad is a black-and-white video of Trump walking down a hall over audio of his warnings against “the deep state,” “warmongers,” “globalists,” “Marxists,” “communists,” and “fascists.”

Trump posted the same video on his Truth Social platform in 2023, but with one difference: Then, the monochromatic ad ended with words on screen calling on the viewer to join Trump’s campaign and fine print saying it was “Paid for by Donald J. Trump for President 2024, Inc.” This time, the 2026 ad says at the bottom: “Paid for by the U.S. Government.”

CNN reported that the ad aired during at least two NFL games on Sunday. CNBC also reported that the ad aired during Fox News Sunday, citing data from advertising intelligence company AdImpact, adding that the TV ad has cost more than $362,000 so far.

A second advert with the same “paid for by the U.S. government” disclaimer began airing on Wednesday. The ad, which featured the song “Love Me” by singer-songwriter JMSN, showed a montage of photos and videos of Trump, intercut with campaign talking points like “largest tax cuts in history” and “reigniting American manufacturing.” This ad, which CNBC reported also aired over the weekend, citing AdImpact data, has cost the federal government nearly $920,000 to date. It also apparently did not get the approval of JMSN, who posted on social media that he “would never authorize my music to be used for ANY political agenda or campaign.”

A third, which is a minute long, features scenic views of Mount Rushmore interspersed with parts of Trump’s speech there for the Fourth of July anniversary.

The ads appear to be part of a campaign blitz ahead of the November midterms, in which the GOP is hoping to defend its majorities in Congress.

Some lawmakers, including from his own Republican Party, are raising concerns with Trump and the White House over the advertisements. Asked about the ads by CBS News on Sunday, Senator John Kennedy of Louisiana said: “I don’t think any public official, including President Trump or Kristi Noem or John Kennedy, should spend public money on private ads for themselves.” (Kennedy was referring to former Homeland Security Secretary Noem, who came under fire for spending $220 million on an advertising campaign for border security.)

When asked about the “Love Me” ad, Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina said that the use of taxpayer money was reminiscent of the far-right former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán. “It’s inappropriate,” Tillis told reporters.

Rep. Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican and a vocal Trump critic, posted on social media about the “Final Battle” ad: “Don’t worry, using taxpayer dollars to run ominous campaign ads of the President has been done before and is completely legal… in banana republics.”

Democrats also raised questions. In a Sept. 24 letter to White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, Sen. Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire demanded answers on the “Love Me” ad’s production cost, the agencies and external contractors involved, the source of funds, and the legal and ethical bases for the spot. Hassan wrote in her letter that the ad “does not have a clear official government purpose and appears to run afoul of federal prohibitions.” Sen. Andy Kim of New Jersey posted to social media about the black-and-white clip: “How much taxpayer money did the government spend on this ad?”

In another Sept. 24 letter, congressional Democrats on appropriations panels wrote to the White House that the “Love Me” ad should be taken off the air, as it was “the sort of government propaganda one might expect in North Korea, not the United States of America, and it is an egregious and illegal misuse of Americans’ hard-earned tax dollars.”

But the White House has defended the ads—which it called, in a Sept. 25 press release, “public service announcements.” A White House official told TIME Friday that the ads weren’t political, didn’t have a call to action, and that the President wasn't on the ballot.

A spokesperson instead said that the ads were “about reminding Americans to love their country and understand what makes it worth defending, at home, at our borders, and abroad.”

Since the 1950s, yearly funding bills—including the appropriations measure the President recently signed—routinely ban the use of taxpayer funds for “publicity or propaganda.”

The Government Accountability Office, which investigates how appropriated funds are spent, has interpreted this to refer to material that is “purely partisan,” “self-aggrandizing,” or “covert.” But it also noted that administrations may need to advocate or defend their policies.

Some lawmakers have pointed to potential violations of the Hatch Act, the 1939 act that limits the political activities of federal civilian employees in the executive branch. The President is exempt from the Hatch Act, though some argue that White House employees who facilitated the airing of the ads aren’t. Last week, the non-profit advocacy group Public Citizen filed a complaint before the GAO and the Office of Special Counsel, which is responsible for overseeing Hatch Act violations, seeking investigation and enforcement of relevant laws.

In defense of the “public service announcements,” the White House has pointed to previous ad campaigns during the administrations of George W. Bush, Barack Obama, and Joe Biden. (During the Bush Administration, one campaign did violate the anti-propaganda measure.)

“When prior Administrations utilized the airwaves, it was called ‘public education,’” the Trump White House said. “When this Administration promotes pride in our country, many of those same voices call it ‘propaganda.’”

title: Rising star Henrich daring to dream of LA Olympics
description: Welsh 400m athlete Charlotte Henrich has her sights set on Los Angeles having found her confidence with a breakthrough summer in 2026.
fullText:
Just 12 months ago, 400-metre runner Charlotte Henrich was celebrating European Under-20 gold in Finland.

Fast forward a year and Henrich is no longer a promising young talent knocking on the door of senior athletics, but an athlete making her mark on the biggest tracks.

Ever since winning bronze with Great Britain in her first senior appearance at the World Athletics Relays in May, she has added accolades in her debut season.

The 20-year-old has become a Welsh record holder, a European Championship and Ultimate Championship silver medallist, and a Commonwealth Games finalist.

And now, Henrich has her sights firmly set on the biggest stage of all - the 2028 Summer Olympics in Los Angeles.

"I really want to go," Henrich told BBC Sport. "Even at Paris 2024, I never watched that event thinking that I could be there.

"I don't think I ever let myself dream that I could be there, and now it feels like a real possibility."

Born in France and raised in Kent after moving to England aged five, Henrich qualifies to represent Wales through her family, who hail from Carmarthen.

Her heritage allowed her to compete for Wales at the Commonwealth Games, where she finished fourth this summer, narrowly missing out on a medal.

Family support has been central to her success so far. By her own admission, she has grappled with self-doubt throughout her young career.

"In school I was very behind and I felt like everyone was a lot better than me," she admitted.

"Every single day I used to come home and say to my dad, 'I am rubbish at everything'.

"Now it's really nice to tell myself that I'm definitely not rubbish at everything."

After winning 400m gold at the 2022 European Under-18 Championships, Henrich felt she placed a "lot of unnecessary pressure" on herself.

"When you do well in your junior career, it can have a bit of a negative effect on your performance because you are so desperate to keep proving," she said.

"After under-18s, everyone was like 'you're under-18 European Champ!', and I didn't want to hear it. I didn't feel that I deserved it."

And though Henrich can now look back on those victories with pride, there are still moments when the youngster feels uneasy.

"It feels a bit abnormal and a bit weird," she said. "It's like, is that me? It feels like the things I've achieved, it's not me who has done it.

"It's just like this person's done this and I'm just here.

"I was talking to Amy [Hunt] at the end of Europeans in the lobby, and I was like, 'you're so cool, you've got four gold medals [at the Commonwealth Games]'."

Hunt's response has stuck with her.

"She told me that I am on this team as well. It was nice that I wasn't just a spectator."

How the race they said women couldn't run took centre stage

Sweeney ad a barrier for girls in sport - Hunt

You would be forgiven for thinking that Henrich's debut season on the senior stage has extinguished any remaining doubt about her ability on the track.

And with so many achievements packed into one season, it is no surprise that she is still trying to process it herself.

It was her impressive anchor leg that earned Great Britain silver in the mixed 4x400 relay at September's Ultimate Championship in Budapest.

That eye-catching result closed out a season in which Henrich shaved over a second off her 400m personal best and proved to herself that she belongs among the best.

"I'm quite proud of the way I manoeuvred it," she said of her silver medal-winning leg in Hungary.

"I was running and I was thinking that I could overtake her. I just had to stay strong.

"When you're on the track, you just kind of go into autopilot. That bit isn't stressful."

Henrich's nod of self-confidence began at the British Championships in June, where she set a Welsh 400m record for the first time.

Having started the year targeting a sub-51 second 400m sprint, Henrich clocked 50.58 to finish third in Birmingham.

In doing so, she beat Michelle Scutt's 44-year record, only to break it again less than a month later by running 0.13 seconds faster at the Diamond League event in London.

"It's been quite an unexpected year," Henrich admitted. "I've definitely gone above and beyond what I thought I could do.

"I knew that this year was going to be hard because the jump was always going to be big."

She said she really believed in herself after the British Championships.

"I ran a big PB, and I was like, 'this is great'," she added.

"I know that I'm still young and there are things that I'll hopefully improve. I'm working really well with my coach.

"This year has been very much me saying, 'let's see what we can do,' and now I've got the experience."

Now Henrich hopes for a "really exciting" future, with her focus firmly on the Los Angeles Olympics, where Wales' rising sprinting star is even allowing herself the chance to dream.

"A lot of people are too scared to dream because if it doesn't happen, it's going to be a big disappointment," she said.

"But now it's cool that I can say I want to be in LA. If I'm not in LA, then I'm going to be so disappointed.

"I've been thinking about LA a lot, and I think I will be thinking about LA for the next two years.

"It would mean a lot, especially because I've been dreaming about this since I was a kid."

title: Seoul demands apology after Zelensky reveals secret North Korean prisoner transfer
description:
— Seoul has called for an official apology from Ukraine after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy revealed what it says was supposed to be a secret transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea.
Zelenskyy told the U.N. General Assembly last week that Ukraine had recently sent the men to South Korea, after capturing them on a Ukraine-Russia battlefield in early 2025. The two are among thousands of North Korean soldiers sent to support Russia’s war against Ukraine.
fullText:
SEOUL, South Korea (AP) — Seoul has called for an official apology from Ukraine after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy revealed what it says was supposed to be a secret transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea.

Zelenskyy told the U.N. General Assembly last week that Ukraine had recently sent the men to South Korea, after capturing them on a Ukraine-Russia battlefield in early 2025. The two are among thousands of North Korean soldiers sent to support Russia's war against Ukraine.

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung quickly accused Ukraine of violating a nondisclosure agreement about the transfer. Ukraine denied making such a deal.

Late Sunday, Seong Ghi-hong, a senior presidential adviser for Lee on public relations, expressed "strong regret" over Ukraine's latest actions and demanded an official apology and explanation.

The South Korean Foreign Ministry on Monday summoned Ukraine's ambassador to Seoul, Andrii Vieshkin, to protest what it described as Kyiv's "unilateral disclosure" of the prisoners' transfer and its false denial that the two countries had agreed to keep the matter confidential.

Vieshkin said he would convey Seoul's position to his government, the ministry said in a statement. Repeated calls to Ukraine's Embassy in Seoul seeking comment were unanswered.

Seong said that Ukraine's "false" denial of the nondisclosure agreement was "an act that seriously undermines trust between the two governments and causes significant damage to friendly relations between the two countries."

Seong said the agreement was reached because Seoul was concerned about the safety of the North Korean soldiers and their relatives in the North while Kyiv worried about possible domestic criticism for forfeiting an opportunity to exchange them for Ukrainian soldiers held in Russia.

While still in Ukraine, the two soldiers said in media interviews that they wanted to resettle in South Korea.

Seoul had called on Ukraine not to send them back to North Korea, where they could face persecution. The South legally regards the North as part of its territory and has a policy of accepting and financially supporting North Korean defectors.

More than 34,000 North Koreans have fled to South Korea since the end of the 1950-53 Korean War, mostly in the last three decades. Most were female civilians from the North's poorer northern provinces. Defections by soldiers are uncommon.

In his U.N. speech, Zelenskyy didn't provide details about the transfer, but said that "one of them, when he realized he was going to ​be taken prisoner, tried to kill himself and he was shocked that ​fate didn't let him die. This is how they raise people in the North."

Some experts say Zelenskyy likely decided to expose the danger of North Korean involvement in the war as a way to attract bigger Western assistance.

Meanwhile, South Korea's liberal government worried that news of the transfer could trigger an angry response from the North and hurt efforts to resume diplomacy between Pyongyang and Washington.

A growing arms exporter with a well-equipped and U.S.-backed military, South Korea has provided humanitarian aid and other support to Ukraine while joining U.S.-led economic sanctions against Russia since its invasion in 2022.

However, Seoul has resisted calls by Kyiv and NATO to provide direct military support to Ukraine in line with a long-standing policy of not supplying weapons to countries actively engaged in conflict.

North Korea and Russia confirmed in April 2025 that their soldiers fought together to repel a Ukrainian incursion into Russia's Kursk border region. South Korea, the United States and others say North Korea has also supplied artillery, ammunition and missiles to Russia in return for economic and military assistance.

South Korea's intelligence service estimated last year that North Korea sent about 15,000 troops and 2,000 of them were killed.

Expanding cooperation with Russia has helped North Korea's leader, Kim Jong Un, push back against U.S.-led pressure and more assertively accelerate a nuclear weapons program. Last month, U.S. President Donald Trump scaled back a military drill with South Korea in an apparent bid to restart diplomacy with Kim, but North Korea has suggested the step wasn't enough to convince it to return to talks.

title: John Fetterman accidentally calls himself a 'lifelong Republican' during an event
description: Senator John Fetterman, Democrat of Pennsylvania, speaks at the Texas Tribune Festival, in Austin, on Saturday.Photograph: Brian Cahn/Zuma Press...
fullText:
With speculation about whether he may defect from the Democratic party swirling around him, the US senator John Fetterman described himself seemingly unintentionally as a "lifelong Republican" during a fireside chat in Texas over the weekend.

Fetterman made the comment when someone listening to him speak with CBS News political correspondent Major Garrett at the Texas Tribune Festival on Saturday asked the Pennsylvania senator why he had not become an independent.

"Because I'm a lifelong Republican," Fetterman replied. Garrett promptly corrected him by saying, "Democrat," as Fetterman raised a hand and shook his head in disbelief.

"That's a moment right there that's clippable, ladies and gentlemen," Garrett said amid laughter from the audience. "Go, go, go – internet, spin wildly! Wildly spin, internet!"

Fetterman then remarked, "Yeah – I guarantee you that's going to break through. That'll get … clipped – yeah. I'm a lifelong Democrat, though, and that's … the point."

Social and news media commenters quickly seized on video of Fetterman's gaffe, with more than one characterizing it as a Freudian slip.

Fetterman has drawn questions over his loyalty to the Democratic party after joining Republicans in opposing his party's efforts to end the US war with Iran as well as to cut off military aid to Israel, which has been accused of committing genocide in Gaza.

He also appeared in a video praising the Republican Pennsylvania US senator Dave McCormick at a convention held by the latter's party in Dallas on 9 September.

Fetterman – who was elected to the US Senate in 2022 – has denied that he intends to defect to the Republican party. He has said he would only abandon the Democrats if they became "the anti-Israel party".

"I'm not going to be a Republican," Fetterman told a reporter at the US Capitol in a video published online by C-Span on 15 September. "Why can't you guys just wait till the midterms? And if I turn a Republican, then I'll be a liar."

At the Texas Tribune Festival on Saturday, Fetterman expressed his belief that it was "entirely possible" for the Democratic party to clinch a majority in the Senate during the federal midterm elections in November, with Republicans being predicted to lose seats in Congress. But he declined to indicate with whom he may side if he ends up holding a tie-breaking vote on any given issue in the 100-seat Senate after the midterms.

"Let's revisit after the midterms, and let's see what happens – you know – if I happen to be 51," said Fetterman, who was elected to the US Senate in 2022. "I don't know."

title: Preston appoint Bradford boss Alexander
description: Preston North End appoint Bradford City boss Graham Alexander as their new manager.
fullText:
Preston North End have appointed Bradford City boss Graham Alexander as their new manager.

The 54-year-old replaces Paul Heckingbottom at Deepdale after he was sacked following six defeats from their opening seven Championship games this season.

Alexander made 372 league appearances across two spells with the Deepdale side as a player.

"It's a special feeling to be named manager of this football club. After speaking to Preston, I knew this was the place I wanted to be," he told the club website., external

'Homecoming' - why Alexander left Bradford for Preston

Will Alexander build on his legacy at Deepdale?

Alexander will be joined at North End by his assistant, and former Preston team-mate, Chris Lucketti.

They return with the club second bottom of the Championship with four points from eight matches.

Bradford, who are top of League One after seven games, confirmed last Thursday that they had "reluctantly" allowed the former Scotland international to speak to the second tier club.

He took over at Valley Parade in November 2023 and won promotion from League Two in his first full season in charge.

They finished fourth in League One in 2025-26 before losing to Bolton Wanderers in the play-offs and have won five of their seven league games this campaign.

"They leave Bradford City in a much stronger position than the one they inherited, with firmer foundations in place for the club to continue moving forward," chief executive Ryan Sparks told the club website., external

"They should be immensely proud of what they have achieved here.

"We will always be grateful for everything they have given the club, and hope our supporters will join us in wishing them and their families nothing but success for the future."

Alexander, who had a brief caretaker spell in charge at Preston in 2011-12, has also had spells in charge of Fleetwood, Scunthorpe, Salford, Motherwell and MK Dons.

His first game as permanent Preston boss will be at home to Millwall on Saturday, 10 October.

fullText:
The valuation on Nvidia (NVDA) is too appetizing for CEO Jensen Huang to ignore any longer.

The king of AI chips revealed a stunning new $150 billion stock buyback plan on Monday — the largest share repurchase authorization increase in history. It brings the company's total buyback authorization to $235 billion.

"NVIDIA's growth is being driven by a once-in-a-generation platform shift to AI and accelerated computing," Huang said in a statement. "Our cash generation gives us the capacity to invest in the technologies that advance this transformation and return capital to shareholders. This authorization reflects our confidence in the long-term opportunity ahead."

Huang likely sees a great moment to buy back Nvidia shares on the cheap, ahead of further acceleration in AI development.

Nvidia's forward price-to-earnings (P/E) multiple has declined steadily since August 2024, when artificial intelligence began to take hold, unleashing a boom in the company's stock price and earnings growth.

The decline has only accelerated this year despite a series of strong quarters.

The forward P/E ratio for Nvidia currently stands at 24 times, not too far removed from the S&P 500's (^GSPC) 20-times multiple, despite the company being one of the fastest-growing companies in corporate America.

title: Republicans' frustrations with Hegseth mount as Iran war costs build
description:
The News
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is running into a wall of congressional GOP resistance as he tries to secure $1.5 trillion for the Pentagon next year.
Lawmakers’ growing reluctance to fulfill Hegseth’s eye-popping budget request reflects real intraparty concerns about his leadership, his relationship with Congress, and the ongoing war with Iran. It also punctuates months of drama at the Pentagon over the ouster and resignation of various top officials, in addition to reports of blocked military promotions.
Hegseth’s fraying ties on the Hill put him on course for a bigger headache after the election, according to interviews with a half-dozen senators as well as multiple administration officials.
fullText:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is running into a wall of congressional GOP resistance as he tries to secure $1.5 trillion for the Pentagon next year.

Lawmakers’ growing reluctance to fulfill Hegseth’s eye-popping budget request reflects real intraparty concerns about his leadership, his relationship with Congress, and the ongoing war with Iran. It also punctuates months of drama at the Pentagon over the ouster and resignation of various top officials, in addition to reports of blocked military promotions.

Hegseth’s fraying ties on the Hill put him on course for a bigger headache after the election, according to interviews with a half-dozen senators as well as multiple administration officials.

“This could turn into a real standoff with the military caught in the middle,” a Trump administration official told Semafor. “The implications: There won’t be money available to pay recruitment bonuses, money to upgrade military housing and repair military housing won’t be there, money to fix ships and aircraft from the war won’t be there, and money to restockpile munitions won’t be there.”

“And the longer this drags out, the more dangerous it becomes, because we’re really depleted after the Iran war,” the official added.

Hegseth is pushing for both a sharp increase in military funding — he’s seeking spending more than 40% higher than last year — and a separate $88 billion to cover costs associated with the Iran war and additional weapons. The Pentagon chief’s expansive needs only heighten some Republicans’ skepticism of his leadership over the US military.

It does not appear that Hegseth has an executable plan to get the hundreds of billions in additional military funding he is requesting in the fall, one Republican senator told Semafor, adding that the lack of permanent civilian nominees to lead the Army and Navy are weighing on the Senate. Hegseth’s preferred pick for Army secretary, Sean Parnell, has faced questions over whether he could even be confirmed by the GOP Senate.

“There are a lot of people that are really upset with the war in Iran and how it’s being played out. We feel it’s hurting our chances in the elections in the fall, and it seems rather haphazard,” said the senator.

“We don’t like what we’re seeing when it comes to the pulling of officers off of the promotion lists,” this senator added. “We don’t like what we see with … indiscriminate firings of admirals and generals across the force.”

Hegseth retains the backing of President Donald Trump, despite his Republican doubters in Congress. Those closest to Trump currently see no chance that Hegseth is replaced. That would leave GOP lawmakers with little choice but to work with him, lest they risk holding up funding the White House says is badly needed.

“The president still is very much in Pete’s corner, but beneath him, there are very serious concerns,” the Trump official said. “Are they going to be able to get any additional money through? Are they going to be able to get any nominees confirmed?”

Most Republicans believe a party-line budget reconciliation bill is the best way to get the Pentagon more money after the election. But getting 50 out of the 53 GOP senators on board for that would be a major challenge.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., who regrets voting to confirm Hegseth, said the secretary’s quandary “comes down to relationships, and I don’t think he’s built strong enough relationships.” Tillis said the first “meaningful briefing” he’s received on Iran occurred last week; the senator subsequently voted against continuing the war, along with three Republican colleagues.

Those four senators alone would be enough to tank a party-line defense spending bill. And given Hegseth’s distance from Congress, Tillis asked Semafor, “why is anybody going to blindly appropriate anything to him?”

“I agree there’s friction,” said Sen. John Kennedy, R-La. “The genesis of that friction is different, depending upon the senator.”

The Trump administration can’t rely on Democrats to pass bipartisan legislation if multiple Republicans are already set to block Hegseth’s request. The secretary, as the administration official noted, is “not going to get Democrat votes — he just can’t do it.”

Kennedy agreed: “Anybody who thinks that we’re going to get money for the Pentagon, which needs it, other than through reconciliation, needs to put down the bong.” He urged Republicans “to sit down and talk about it.”

Hegseth’s supporters also acknowledge a rift that’s damaging the Pentagon’s ability to get what it wants. Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., said in an interview that the continued lack of engagement with Democrats “continues to be a strategic error” for Hegseth and his team.

“Republicans are frustrated that he hasn’t reached out to Democrats. He didn’t in his confirmation, and he hasn’t much since at all,” Cramer said.

Kingsley Wilson, a spokesperson for the Pentagon, said the administration conducted over 500 briefings on the budget request — some of them bipartisan — and said the department is “in lockstep with the Republican conference in Congress to achieve the President’s historic investment in defense.”

The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

At the heart of the GOP frustration with Hegseth is his handling of military firings and promotions. Cramer supports much of what the secretary has done but acknowledged the turbulence has “bothered some people.

“And it probably has had an impact on morale a little bit,” Cramer added. “But all in all, I think Pete’s a pretty strong leader.”

Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, worked to arrange a bipartisan classified briefing about the administration’s funding request last week. The Senate Armed Services Committee also heard closed testimony from Hegseth’s top deputies, including Deputy Defense Secretary Stephen Feinberg.

But Collins is cool to another party-line bill. “I don’t like reconciliation, period,” she told Semafor — and Hegseth, who she voted against.

“One of my concerns, which unfortunately has been borne out, was that he would fire a lot of very capable military officials, and he has done that. He has blocked promotions for some of our most capable military officers,” Collins said. “The number of women and Black people that had been struck from the list was awful.”

“He also is not the most respectful when it comes to Congress’ role,” she added. It’s something Republicans are urging Hegseth to fix.

Sen. Tim Sheehy, R-Mont., started prodding the Pentagon to go into sell mode last winter. He said he believes the $1.5 trillion top-line number is needed to maintain military superiority but said the administration has got “to communicate that better” to Congress.

“You’ve got to come up here and sell your vision to the board of directors of America, which is us,” Sheehy said. “Everyone has every right to be skeptical … [the Pentagon’s] been almost a symbol of bureaucratic dysfunction. It’s not quite Somali fraud in Minnesota, but it’s been some pretty dumb sh*t we spent money on.”

The upcoming election isn’t necessarily going to bring relief to Hegseth; in fact it might be the opposite, if Republicans lose serious ground in the midterms.

Several of the party’s candidates are now campaigning to end the Iran war, and it’s hard to see where 50 Senate votes for more funding will come from right now. And that’s not even getting into the fractious House.

Trump’s continued backing of Hegseth sets up a choice for Republicans, who have no realistic shot of ousting the defense secretary. They’ll have to decide whether to risk his ire (and military readiness) or hold their nose and vote the money through this year.

Because if Democrats take either chamber of Congress, it appears more military funding is off the table until the war ends.

title: Australia-born Strange in England World Cup squad
description: Australia-born second-row forward Jasmin Strange is one of four potential debutants in England's 23-strong squad for the World Cup.
fullText:
Australia-born Jasmin Strange is one of four potential debutants in England's 23-strong squad for the World Cup.

Sydney Roosters second-row forward Strange, who is set to play in Sunday's NRLW Grand Final against Brisbane Broncos, has committed herself to England, for whom she qualifies through her mother Adele.

The 23-year-old is the daughter of Roosters women's head coach John Strange, who played for Featherstone in the 1990s.

Strange is joined by three uncapped players - Leeds Rhinos' Connie Boyd, Hope Millard of Canterbury Bulldogs, and Wigan Warriors' Lucie Sams.

In addition to Strange and Millard, whose father Shane was a forward for Widnes, Leeds and Wigan, three other NRLW players have made the squad - including dual code international Fran Goldthorp, who last played rugby league for her country at the most recent World Cup in 2022.

Newcastle Knights' Georgia Roche and Hollie-Mae Dodd of Canberra Raiders have also been included.

Strange's inclusion as a heritage player - one who qualifies through parentage - comes after eligibility rules were relaxed this year.

An International Rugby League ruling means that players can now represent more than one of the three tier one nations - Australia, New Zealand and England.

That led to speculation that head coach Stu Barrow might call on more heritage players with NRLW experience - such as Roosters playmaker Jocelyn Kelleher, Bulldogs half-back Tayla Preston and Wests Tigers full-back Caitlin Turnbull.

But Barrow has said he wants to give homegrown players an opportunity to develop.

All three Woman of Steel nominees - Jenna Foubister, Eva Hunter and Megan Williams - have been selected, along with six of their Wigan team-mates. Grand Final winners York Valkyrie have one player in the squad in forward Liv Wood.

Loose forward Jodie Cunningham, who will retire after the World Cup, is selected along with St Helens team-mate Vicky Whitfield, who will be competing at her fourth World Cup.

Barrow said: "Narrowing our squad from 40 players to a final 23 has involved some difficult decisions, but we believe we have the right balance of experience and youth to compete on the world stage.

"It's also an exciting moment for the programme with the inclusion of Australian-based heritage players for the first time."

This year's men's, women's and wheelchair World Cups will run concurrently, with England competing in all three. The wheelchair squad was announced last week, while the men's squad will be confirmed on 5 October.

The tournaments are being staged largely in Australia, with Papua New Guinea's men and women each playing two pool matches in their own country, and their New Zealand counterparts playing one.

England face three group matches - beginning in Perth against Wales on 17 October and Australia on 24 October, before facing Samoa in Wollongong on 30 October.

The top two sides in England's four-team group will go through to the semi-finals on 7 and 8 November, with the final on 15 November.

title: President Trump announces new $15 billion steel plant to be built in Iowa
description:
Washington — President Trump on Monday announced that the company Mesabi Metallics will build a $15 billion steel plant in Iowa over the coming years, in what would be the largest of its kind in U.S. history. 
"There's a company known as Mesabi," the president said in the Oval Office. "And they're going to make a big investment in a place called Iowa.
fullText:
Washington — President Trump on Monday announced that the company Mesabi Metallics will build a $15 billion steel plant in Iowa over the coming years, in what would be the largest of its kind in U.S. history.

"There's a company known as Mesabi," the president said in the Oval Office. "And they're going to make a big investment in a place called Iowa. I love Iowa. I won Iowa every time. Today, we're thrilled to announce that Mesabi Metallics will be building the largest steel plant in American history in the great state of Iowa."

The president and the Minnesota-based Mesabi Metallics unveiled the company's plans for what the White House is calling a mega steel plant, alongside Mesabi executives and Iowa officials. The announcement comes as several Iowa Republicans face competitive elections in the November midterms, including the party's candidates for Senate and governor.

Although Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said Monday the steel plant won't receive direct federal support, he acknowledged that the government-run Export-Import Bank financed Mesabi's iron ore plant in Minnesota, which will provide the raw materials essential to making steel.

Once it's up and running in 2030, the plant is expected to produce 7.5 million or more tons of steel per year. A White House official said the plant is expected to create 1,750 permanent jobs in Iowa.

The plans for a new plant mark the Trump administration's latest move to boost domestic steel manufacturing in the face of overseas competition, a centerpiece of the president's trade agenda. Last year, he doubled tariffs on imported steel to 50%, and steel levies have been part of the ongoing trade dispute between the U.S. and Canada. He also approved a deal for Japan-based Nippon Steel to buy U.S. Steel, an arrangement that calls for new investments in the iconic Pittsburgh-based company.

Mesabi has not announced where in Iowa the steel plant will be, but Energy Secretary Chris Wright mentioned that it would be in the southeast part of the state. A White House official said this will be the first mega steel plant built in the U.S. since the 1960s. The Trump administration expects the steel could support U.S. defense projects in the future. The Wall Street Journal was first to report the president's anticipated announcement of the new steel plant.

The Export-Import Bank's board approved a $770 million direct loan to Mesabi Metallics for its iron ore endeavors on Sept. 24, a spokesperson for EXIM told CBS News. The board was initially considering up to $10 billion in support, according to a March news release.

Mesabi Metallics is owned by India-based Essar Group, but its operations haven't always been known as Mesabi Metallics.

In 2008, the Essar Group's Essar Steel Minnesota LLC began work on a massive iron mine and processing facility in Minnesota. But after years of delays, missed deadlines and financial challenges, Essar Steel Minnesota LLC filed for bankruptcy in 2016. Frustrated with the delays, the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources took steps in 2019 to potentially bar Essar Global from working with the state, although the company sued over that move, and the state ultimately did not complete the debarment process.

"This is a step in the right direction after northern Minnesotans have waited patiently — too patiently, in fact — for economic gains that have been dangled in front of their eyes for many years," Democratic state Reps. Julie Sandstede and Rob Ecklund said in a statement at the time.

What was known as Essar Steel Minnesota LLC was eventually reborn from the ashes of bankruptcy and was bought by Chippewa Capital Partners. But Essar Group eventually regained control starting in 2019.

CBS News has reached out to Mesabi Metallics and the Essar Group for comment.

State aid could potentially be on the way for Mesabi Metallics, too.

The Des Moines Register reported state lawmakers are being alerted they may need to return to the statehouse to approve tax breaks for Mesabi. CBS News has reached out to top members of the Iowa statehouse for comment.

"I'm so excited about this project," Iowa Sen. Joni Ernst said, thanking Mr. Trump and Essar.

It's not clear why the steel plant is in Iowa, instead of Minnesota, closer to the iron ore mine.

Iowa Republicans are facing competitive races for the U.S. House, Senate and governor's mansion. Republicans, who currently hold the governor's mansion and both Senate seats, are trying to fend off Democrats from changing that.

In the governor's race, Democratic Iowa State Auditor Rob Sand is facing off against Republican businessman Zach Lahn in what's expected to be a close race. In the open U.S. Senate seat being vacated by Sen. Joni Ernst's departure, Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson faces Democratic state lawmaker Josh Turek.

In the House, there are closely watched races in two Iowa congressional districts, between Republican Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Democratic former state Rep. Christina Bohannan, and between Republican Rep. Zach Nunn and Democratic state Sen. Sarah Trone Garriott.

Mr. Trump gave Hinson a shoutout in the Oval Office Monday, saying she will be "hopefully elected to the Senate, and she's outstanding." The president said he'll visit Iowa for a "great rally" there before the midterms.

A reporter asked the president why Republicans are having to work so hard to win seats in Iowa, a state he won by 13 points. The president said he thinks the polls, which show close statewide races in the Hawkeye State, are inaccurate.

"I don't know, I love Iowa," he said. "I've always been very strong with Iowa."

title: Konsa and O'Reilly doubtful for England as Tuchel expects morning decision
description: Ezri Konsa and Nico O'Reilly are both doubts to play in England's Nations League match against the Czech Republic on Tuesday night.
fullText:
Ezri Konsa and Nico O'Reilly are both doubts to play in England's Nations League match against the Czech Republic on Tuesday night.

The pair were the only two members of the England squad to miss training on Monday morning, with the players following their own individual programmes.

Both played the full 90 minutes in England's 3-2 loss to Spain on Saturday.

And Thomas Tuchel does not yet know if the two players will be available for the match.

"I'm not sure yet, they missed training, so that's what you saw, because of minor issues, but there are still issues and they need to be assessed and take a decision tomorrow morning," Tuchel said.

Manchester City's O'Reilly started at left-back, a position he made his own during the World Cup, and his absence would open an opportunity for Lewis Hall to play.

It was O'Reilly's mistake which led to Alex Baena drawing Spain level at 2-2 at Wembley before the World Cup winners went on to claim victory.

Arsenal centre-back Konsa has become one of Tuchel's most trusted players and started seven of the eight matches at the World Cup.

Central defender Jarrad Branthwaite came on for Marc Guehi late on against Spain and could be a contender to start if Konsa is unavailable.

England play four matches in this international window and, after the loss to Spain, take on the Czech Republic both home and away, either side of travelling to Rijeka to play Croatia.

Tuchel rues 'big mistakes' - did Man City charges have impact?

England embrace the chaos - but control also needed to win big prizes

Before the loss to Spain at Wembley on Saturday, there was a lot of debate about England's style of play and identity.

Barcelona forward Anthony Gordon said the Three Lions should play a more traditional way, while Tuchel said he may start to "embrace the chaos".

England came from behind to lead Spain 2-1, with Harry Kane then missing a penalty before the world champions scored twice to win the match 3-2.

"I think we showed our style, and showed our courage and identity - they showed it throughout the 90 minutes," said Tuchel.

"I think we were a valid part of a very good football match overall, over 90 minutes both teams showed our quality.

"We caused ourselves some problems with individual mistakes. It should not happen, but it happened.

"But I think we played our way, and we encouraged the players to play their way, and the way they want to play."

The matches England are playing in the Nations League come in the new format of an international break which will bring the team together for three weeks.

And Tuchel, who has to prepare the players for four games in 11 days, said he has found having the matches in a short period of time difficult.

"I find this format now even more challenging than any other format, I have to say, a lot of travelling and playing twice within only two days of rest in between and then flying and a change of pitches," added the German.

"I think the change of training in itself, the change of training style, the change of style of play, sometimes the change of position for a player between national team and club brings its own risks for injury, and I think this format is my feeling at the moment, it increases it more than decreases."

title: Ferguson retains Rangers dream but Bologna exit never close
description: Lewis Ferguson reveals "nothing was ever that close" on a move away from Bologna this summer amid reports of interest from Rangers but he does harbour ambitions of a return to his boyhood club.
fullText:
Lewis Ferguson says he was never close to leaving Bologna this summer amid reports of interest from boyhood club Rangers.

But the Scotland midfielder, 27, does retain aspirations of an Ibrox return at some stage in his career.

Ferguson was released by Rangers at 14 and made his way to Serie A in 2022, via Hamilton Academical and Aberdeen.

He has captained Bologna since 2023 and led them to their first Coppa Italia in over 50 years in 2025.

However, starts became sparse last term under Vincenzo Italiano, making just 17 in the league.

Asked about links to Rangers, Ferguson said: "I had a long think after the World Cup about my future and I was a little bit unsure but nothing was ever that close."

Pocognoli has no concern over Scotland's lack of goals

From shaky start to statement wins - 100 days of McInnes at Rangers

And he added: "When I went back for pre-season, we had a new manager [Domenico Tedesco] and it was like a fresh start.

"We changed again since [with Raffaele Palladino], so I've had three new managers in the last two months [including Sebastien Pocognoli with Scotland].

"I had a long think about what my future was going to look like and in the end it was still at Bologna.

"I've loved every moment that I've had there. It was just about continuing that journey and seeing where it takes me."

Ferguson, who is under contract until 2028 with the option of a further year, has played every minute of Bologna's five Serie A games so far this season.

His father, Derek, and uncle, Barry, both played for Rangers with the latter captaining and at one stage managing at Ibrox.

In July, newly-installed Rangers manager Derek McInnes spoke of an "obvious link" with Ferguson, having worked with the player at Aberdeen.

On his bond with Rangers, Ferguson said: "It's no secret that I grew up a fan and my family is involved in the club.

"It was a dream of mine as a kid and that's not changed but I don't want to speak about that while I'm a player at Bologna.

"In the future, you never know. It might happen, it might not, but it's always been something in the back of mind."

title: Newcastle agree delay to Fineanganofo arrival
description: Free-scoring All Blacks wing Fehi Fineanganofo convinces Newcastle Red Bulls to delay his arrival on Tyneside so he can chase his dream of playing at the Rugby World Cup.
fullText:
Free-scoring All Blacks wing Fehi Fineanganofo has convinced Newcastle Red Bulls to delay his arrival on Tyneside so he can chase his dream of playing at the Rugby World Cup.

It was originally announced back in January that the 24-year-old had agreed a two-year deal with Newcastle, beginning at the start of the current campaign.

However, Fineanganofo's exceptional form with the Wellington-based Hurricanes in Super Rugby then propelled him into Test reckoning.

He made his New Zealand debut against France in July.

Under All Blacks selection rules, a move overseas this year would have put Fineanganofo's emerging international career on ice and ruled him out of contention for the Rugby World Cup, which begins in October 2027.

Newcastle have therefore allowed Fineanganofo to stay with the Hurricanes, for whom he broke the record for the most tries in a single Super Rugby campaign this year, for an extra season.

His Newcastle deal is still for two campaigns, but now covers the 2027-28 and 2028-29 seasons instead.

"I'm really grateful to Newcastle Red Bulls for the support and understanding they've shown me," said Fineanganofo.

"The opportunity to stay in New Zealand and push for selection for the Rugby World Cup means a huge amount, and I'm fully committed to joining the club after the tournament and giving everything I can to the team."

Newcastle's sporting general manager Neil McIlroy said: "We are fully supportive of Fehi's desire to represent his country at Rugby World Cup 2027, which marries with our own philosophy of aiming high and enabling our athletes to achieve their ambitions.

"Fehi's arrival in 2027, with additional international experience that will only add to his already devastating qualities as a top-class winger, is another statement of intent around where this club is going."

The compromise ends long-running uncertainty about Fineanganofo's future.

In June, New Zealand Rugby denied they were attempting to put together a deal to get Fineanganofo out of his Newcastle contract.

Just a few weeks ago, Red Bulls' head coach Dan McFarland said he expected Fineanganofo to arrive in November and play in the current campaign.

His side began the Prem season with former Ulster man Werner Kok, signed in June as doubts over Fineanganofo's move increased, and 35-year-old Christian Wade as their first-choice wings.

McIlroy kept open the possibility of adding to the club's options in that position.

"We are more than happy with the quality and depth that our existing squad possesses, but may yet choose to add to the outside back position if a player of the required standard becomes available," he said.

Newcastle lost 59-26 away to defending champions Northampton on Friday in their league opener, and will take on Leicester at home on Saturday.

title: O'Sullivan knocked out of Shenzhen Open
description: Seven-time world champion Ronnie O'Sullivan, world number one Zhao Xintong and defending champion Mark Williams lose on the opening day of the Shenzhen Open.
fullText:
Seven-time world champion Ronnie O'Sullivan, world number one Zhao Xintong and defending champion Mark Williams were knocked out on the opening day of the Shenzhen Open.

China's Jiang Jun, who is 64th in the world rankings, took the opening two frames before England's O'Sullivan levelled with breaks of 92 and 52.

Jiang reeled off the next three frames, sealing a famous 5-2 second-round win with a superb break of 108 to set up a meeting with Englishman Zak Surety.

Scott Donaldson stunned 2025 world champion Zhao by winning a final-frame decider.

Scotland's Donaldson, who is 65 places below Zhao in the rankings, compiled breaks of 77, 105, 50 and 62 as he came from 3-2 down.

Donaldson will take on China's Pang Junxu in round three.

Welshman Williams lost 5-4 to China's Fan Zhengyi after fouling on the final pink.

England's Judd Trump cruised to a 5-0 win over China's Huang Jiahao and goes into the last 16 after Anthony McGill, his scheduled third-round opponent, withdrew on medical grounds.

In Monday's other second-round encounters, Australia's Neil Robertson beat China's Liu Hongyu 5-2, England's Chris Wakelin claimed a 5-3 win over Welshman Liam Davies and China's Si Jiahui swept to a 5-1 success against England's Oliver Lines.

Belgium's Ben Mertens also progressed as Northern Ireland's Mark Allen withdrew for personal reasons.

Wales' Jamie Clarke, England's Andrew Higginson, Hong Kong's Marco Fu and England's Sam Craigie progressed in the first-round matches that took place on Monday.

title: Stocks fall as surging interest rates add another worry for investors
description:
By midmorning, the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield had risen to 5.27%, its highest level since mid-June 2007. (Samuel Corum / Bloomberg via Getty Images file)
Stocks fell Monday alongside a jump in bond yields and erratic oil trading as geopolitical upheaval remained front and center for traders.
fullText:
Stocks fell Monday alongside a jump in bond yields and erratic oil trading as geopolitical upheaval remained front and center for traders.

The S&P 500 ended lower by 0.7% and the Nasdaq Composite dropped 0.9% as oil prices rose, pushing Brent crude oil back above $106 per barrel.

Earlier in the day, Brent rose beyond $108, but the jump moderated after reports said mediators planned to meet with U.S. and Iranian officials separately to discuss the stalemate between the two sides over the war with Iran. Iran’s semiofficial ISNA news agency downplayed the significance of the meetings, saying that Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, would attend talks with mediators but that no U.S. representatives would be present.

Other reports throughout the day that said President Donald Trump was open to offering Iran economic concessions to reboot talks and reach a deal also took some of the heat off oil prices. NBC News has not confirmed those reports.

Over the weekend, Trump said he had rejected a recent proposal from Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, through which critical energy supplies flowed before the war.

“They want to make a deal, and I think that’s fine,” Trump told reporters in Washington. “I like making a deal too, but ... that deal would not be acceptable.”

Monday’s rocky oil trading has been a familiar feature of this year’s turbulent markets.

Bond yields also surged to fresh multiyear highs.

The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield rose as high as 5.27%, its highest since mid-June 2007. A wide swath of other Treasurys also continued to trade above 5%, and the yield on the 30-year bond hit its highest level since May 2004.

The 2-year Treasury, which is often viewed as a signal of where the market expects central bank rates to go, reached its highest level since 2024.

Market watchers’ anxiety has grown alongside the rise in bond yields.

“The significant increase in oil prices so far this year hasn’t knocked the wind out of the global economy’s sails,” longtime market analyst Ed Yardeni wrote Saturday. “The question is whether rapidly rising interest rates will do so.”

“Unfortunately, these higher rates also exacerbate the outlook for large government deficits worldwide,” wrote Yardeni, president of Yardeni Research.

Still, stocks have largely remained resilient in the face of rising inflation from higher oil prices and bond yields that keep shooting higher.

Part of the reason “is that financial conditions have changed little” since January, analysts at Goldman Sachs said. They added that “the substantial rise in interest rates has been nearly offset by the effects of higher equity prices.”

But the equity market’s rise this year has been driven primarily by just a few sectors, which troubles some analysts.

For the year so far, the S&P 500 has risen a little more than 12%. But a look under the hood reveals a different story. The information technology sector has gained 27% this year, and the energy sector has added 38%.

The healthcare, industrials and materials sectors are up 10%. But the real estate, consumer staples and communication services sectors have all gained less than 7%. The utilities, financial and consumer discretionary sectors have all contracted.

On top of higher oil prices, rising bond yields and geopolitical headlines that could swing stocks in either direction at a moment’s notice, the end of the month features prominent central bank meetings, including meetings at the Federal Reserve, where rates could rise further.

title: Number of measles cases nears 3,700 — with the epicenter in Pennsylvania
description:
The growing number of measles cases across the U.S. this year is nearing 3,700, federal data shows, as an outbreak in Pennsylvania continues to surge. 
There are now 3,659 confirmed cases this year, according to the latest update from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. 
That total includes new cases from Pennsylvania, where 129 cases have been reported over the past seven days, a dashboard from Pennsylvania’s health department shows, bringing the total to 890.
fullText:
The growing number of measles cases across the U.S. this year is nearing 3,700, federal data shows, as an outbreak in Pennsylvania continues to surge.

There are now 3,659 confirmed cases this year, according to the latest update from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

That total includes new cases from Pennsylvania, where 129 cases have been reported over the past seven days, a dashboard from Pennsylvania’s health department shows, bringing the total to 890.

Possible measles exposures have been traced to the Philadelphia International Airport and the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia.

The updates come as the Trump administration and Pennsylvania leaders have sparred over measles-associated deaths — the first in the U.S. this year.

While the CDC only shows one death on its website, Pennsylvania has reported four measles-associated deaths.

The CDC says it will update data "as additional information becomes available and relevant reviews are completed."

The deaths include a 40-year-old woman with an active infection, an 18-year-old with a rare neurological complication from infection, and two infants, including a newborn with a spleen laceration.

The Trump administration’s Department of Health and Human Services did not comment on whether the agency has received any updated information that could change its current death count, but said the one reported death was verified by the National Center for Health Statistics.

“CDC is also working with the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists (CSTE) to develop a standardized case definition for deaths due to measles,” the department told The Independent in an email on Monday. “This work is intended to promote consistent classification and reporting of measles deaths across jurisdictions.”

HHS Sec. Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. said the CDC would pull data for measles death counts in early September: a break from updating information about deaths after notifications from state officials.

Regardless of the deaths listed by the CDC, this year’s measles resurgence has been historic.

It’s been the most active year for measles since the 1990s, the American Medical Association notes, before the contagious virus was declared eliminated from the U.S. in 2000.

There have been 40 outbreaks reported nationwide this year, with 95 percent of confirmed cases tied to outbreaks in 2025 or 2026.

The majority of cases – including all of the reported Pennsylvania deaths – have been reported in unvaccinated individuals.

Two doses of the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine provide 97 percent protection against infection, but experts say vaccine hesitancy and misinformation have helped child vaccination rates fall.

Without it, infections spread easily after a person with measles coughs or sneezes.

The viral droplets they produce can linger in the air for up to two hours or contaminate surfaces.

Signs of infection include fever that may spike to more than 104 degrees Fahrenheit (40 degrees Celsius), a rash, a cough, a runny nose and red, watery eyes.

People with the disease begin to feel sick around a week or two after they come into contact with the virus.
